title: “MY PASTOR SAID NO.” BUT DID GOD?
paragraphs:
“MY PASTOR SAID NO.” BUT DID GOD?
Does the Bible Really Teach That You Need a Pastor’s Permission for Major Life Decisions—or Have We Confused Godly Shepherding With Control?
There is a sentence some Christians are terrified to say out loud.
“My pastor told me not to do it… but I don’t know if God actually said no.”
Maybe it was marriage.
A career.
Moving to another city.
Leaving a ministry position.
Starting a business.
Changing churches.
Going to Bible school.
Accepting an opportunity.
Or making some other decision that could alter the direction of your life.
You prayed. You searched Scripture. You tried to examine your motives. You sought counsel.
Then someone asked the question that suddenly made you feel spiritually guilty:
“But did your pastor give you permission?”
And now something inside you is trembling.
Because you love God.
You respect spiritual leadership.
You do not want to become rebellious.

You have heard stories about people who “went against their pastor” and supposedly destroyed their lives. You have heard Hebrews 13:17 quoted: “Obey your leaders and submit to them.” You have been warned about “touching God’s anointed.” Perhaps you were even taught that moving forward without pastoral approval means moving outside God’s covering.
So now you are not merely asking whether your decision is wise.
You are wondering whether disagreeing with your pastor means disagreeing with God.
That is a much heavier burden.
And before we go any further, hear this carefully:
This article is not an attack on pastors.

Faithful pastors are gifts to Christ’s church. They teach, counsel, protect, correct, encourage, pray, warn, suffer quietly, carry burdens nobody sees, and sometimes lie awake thinking about people who barely realize how deeply their shepherd loves them.
Scripture commands Christians to respect godly leadership.
Scripture commands Christians to receive correction.
Scripture praises wisdom that seeks counsel.
Scripture condemns arrogance, stubbornness, divisiveness, and rebellion.
So this is not permission to become unteachable.
But Scripture also does something else.
It places every shepherd beneath the Chief Shepherd.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
That distinction changes everything.
The question is not, “Should Christians listen to their pastors?”
Absolutely.
The deeper question is:
Does the Bible give a pastor universal veto authority over the ordinary personal decisions of another adult Christian?
When we examine Scripture carefully, the answer requires more nuance than either extreme allows.
Hebrews 13:17 is usually where the conversation begins:
“Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls…”
The Greek begins:
Πείθεσθε τοῖς ἡγουμένοις ὑμῶν καὶ ὑπείκετε
Peithesthe tois hēgoumenois hymōn kai hypeikete.
The words are significant.

Πείθεσθε — peithesthe comes from peithō, a word associated with persuading, being convinced, trusting, or yielding in response to persuasion. In Hebrews 13:17 it functions as an imperative and is commonly and legitimately translated “obey.” ὑπείκετε — hypeikete carries the idea of yielding or submitting.
So we should not weaken the verse until submission means nothing.
There really is biblical authority in the church.
There really is a responsibility to follow faithful spiritual leadership.
But notice what the verse says immediately afterward.
These leaders “keep watch over your souls” and will “give an account.”
The authority described here is therefore not the authority of an owner.
It is the responsibility of a steward.
The shepherd watches because the sheep belong to Someone Else.
And that Someone Else is Christ.
The New Testament never tells pastors, “These people belong to you.”
Peter says almost the opposite.
Writing to elders, he tells them to shepherd God’s flock, exercising oversight willingly and eagerly, but “not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2–3).
Then Peter identifies the One above every earthly shepherd:
“the Chief Shepherd” (1 Peter 5:4).
That title belongs to Jesus.
Your pastor may be your shepherd.
But your pastor has a Shepherd.
Your pastor may exercise authority.
But your pastor remains under authority.
Your pastor may give counsel.
But your pastor does not become your conscience.
Your pastor may warn you.
He may correct you.
He may tell you that he believes you are making a terrible mistake.
And sometimes—please hear this—he may be right.
Sometimes the thing we call “control” is actually correction we do not want to hear.
Sometimes the pastor is not manipulating us at all.
Sometimes we are simply angry because someone loved us enough to confront our sin.
If Scripture clearly calls something sin, “God told me” cannot make it holy.

If you are committing adultery, stealing, lying, abandoning biblical responsibilities, practicing sexual immorality, pursuing greed, cultivating hatred, or deliberately violating the commands of Christ, you do not get to hide behind “personal conviction.”
God will never lead you contrary to what He has already revealed in His Word.
That matters enormously.
But there is another danger.
It is possible to turn legitimate spiritual authority into something Scripture never authorized.
Paul himself wrote something astonishing to the Corinthians:
οὐχ ὅτι κυριεύομεν ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως
ouch hoti kyrieuomen hymōn tēs pisteōs
In 2 Corinthians 1:24, Paul says, in essence:
“Not that we lord it over your faith.”
The verb κυριεύομεν — kyrieuomen comes from kyrieuō, carrying the sense of exercising lordship or dominion.
Think about who is saying this.
Paul.
An apostle.
A man personally commissioned by the risen Christ.
A man through whom the Holy Spirit gave inspired Scripture to the church.
And yet Paul deliberately distinguishes apostolic ministry from lording over another believer’s faith.
Instead, he says they are “fellow workers” for the believers’ joy.
That should stop us.
If Paul could describe ministry that way, pastors should be very careful about language that effectively communicates:
“You cannot make this decision unless I authorize it.”
And Christians should be equally careful before handing another human being authority Christ never commanded them to surrender.
Jesus Himself established the pattern.
When the disciples became fascinated with power, Jesus pointed toward Gentile rulers who “lord it over” others.
Then He said:
“It shall not be so among you.”
Christian leadership was supposed to look different.
Greatness in Christ’s kingdom bends downward.
It serves.
It sacrifices.
It washes feet.
It carries burdens.
And ultimately it looks like Jesus Christ, who said that the Son of Man came “not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:25–28).
That is the shape of Christian authority.
Not domination.
Cruciform service.
A faithful pastor should increasingly help you depend upon Jesus—not increasingly make you incapable of functioning without the pastor’s personal approval.
That does not mean spiritual independence.
Biblical Christianity knows nothing of the arrogant believer who says, “Nobody can tell me anything. It’s just me and Jesus.”
That attitude is dangerous too.
Proverbs repeatedly praises counsel:
“Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety” (Proverbs 11:14).
And:
“Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22).
Notice something beautiful.
Scripture says counselors.
Advisers.
Plural.
Wisdom welcomes voices.
Wisdom listens.
Wisdom does not surround itself exclusively with people who say what it wants to hear.
A mature believer should be able to sit before a pastor and say:
“Please tell me if you see something I am missing.”
That is not weakness.
That is wisdom.
A mature believer should be able to hear:
“I love you, but I think you are making a mistake.”

And instead of immediately shouting, “You’re controlling me!” the believer should go home, pray, open Scripture, examine motives, seek additional mature counsel, and ask God whether pride is making correction difficult to receive.
But counsel and permission are not identical.
That distinction may save someone reading this from two completely different disasters.
One disaster is rebellion disguised as freedom.
The other is control disguised as submission.
Neither resembles Jesus.
Consider the Bereans.
Paul preached to them, and Acts 17:11 says they received the message eagerly while “examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so.”
They tested the teaching of an apostle against Scripture.
And Luke calls them noble for doing it.
Think about that.
They did not dishonor Paul by opening their Bibles.
They honored truth.
Biblical submission does not require you to turn off discernment.
Biblical authority does not fear an open Bible.
A healthy pastor should be able to say:
“Do not believe something merely because I said it. Search the Scriptures. Follow Christ.”
That kind of pastor is not losing authority.
He is demonstrating it properly.
And this becomes especially important when Christians make major decisions.
Should you seek pastoral counsel before marriage?
Often, yes. Strongly.
Marriage is enormous. A wise pastor may see character issues romantic emotion has blinded you to.
But Scripture does not establish a universal rule saying every adult Christian marriage requires a pastor’s personal authorization to become morally legitimate before God.
Should you seek counsel before moving?
Certainly it can be wise.
A pastor may see spiritual, family, financial, or relational consequences you have overlooked.
But there is no New Testament command saying an adult believer may not relocate without pastoral permission.
Should you seek counsel before changing churches?
Absolutely.
Leaving in anger, bitterness, unresolved conflict, or resistance to legitimate discipline can reveal serious spiritual problems.
But no pastor owns a Christian.
Christ does.
Should you seek counsel before starting a ministry, changing careers, accepting a job, entering school, launching a business, or making another life-altering decision?
Wisdom says:
Do not despise godly counsel.
Humility says:
Listen carefully.
Love says:
Honor faithful shepherds.
Discernment says:
Test everything by Scripture.
Responsibility says:
You will ultimately answer to God for your obedience.
That last sentence can be terrifying.
Because sometimes we secretly want someone else to make every decision for us.
If the pastor chooses, then perhaps the pastor can carry the blame if everything collapses.
But spiritual maturity does not mean outsourcing your conscience.
There are matters where Scripture gives direct commands.
Obey them.
There are matters where Scripture gives principles.
Apply them prayerfully.
There are matters of wisdom where multiple choices may be morally permissible.
Seek counsel.
Examine your motives.
Count the cost.
Consider your responsibilities.
Listen to mature believers.
Pray.
Search Scripture.
And then walk before God with a clear conscience.
Romans 14 is especially illuminating because Paul addresses disputed matters among believers. His answer is not to appoint one Christian as the conscience of every other Christian.
He repeatedly brings the believer back before the Lord.
“Each of us will give an account of himself to God” (Romans 14:12).
That sentence destroys both pride and unhealthy dependence.
You belong to Jesus.
Which means you are not free to do whatever you want.
But it also means no human being becomes Jesus for you.
There is only one Lord of the conscience.
Christ.
There is only one Head of the church.
Christ.
There is only one Savior whose blood purchased you.
Christ.
There is only one Mediator between God and humanity.
Christ Jesus.
Your pastor did not die for your sins.
Jesus did.
Your pastor did not rise from the grave.
Jesus did.
Your pastor will not sit upon the throne at the final judgment.
Jesus will.
And any faithful pastor reading those words should be able to say:
Amen.
Because healthy shepherds do not want Christ’s throne.
They want people at Christ’s feet.
This is where the subject becomes painfully personal.
Maybe someone used spiritual authority to frighten you.
Maybe every disagreement was called rebellion.
Maybe questions were treated as betrayal.
Maybe leaving was described as abandoning God.
Maybe “submission” meant never saying no.
Maybe you learned to distrust your own ability to read Scripture because you were told only the leader could properly hear from God.
If that happened, do not respond by running into the opposite ditch.
Do not let abusive authority make you hate biblical authority.
Do not let a controlling shepherd make you suspicious of every shepherd.
Do not let wounds turn into permanent rebellion.
Jesus can heal what people misrepresented.
And perhaps the harder possibility is this:
Maybe your pastor was not controlling you.
Maybe he was warning you.
Maybe you called it manipulation because the truth hurt.
Maybe mature believers have repeatedly told you the relationship is unhealthy.
Maybe everyone who loves Jesus and genuinely knows you sees danger, but you have decided that anyone who disagrees with you “doesn’t understand what God told me.”
That should frighten you too.
Because refusing every warning is not spiritual maturity.
Sometimes God protects us through counsel.
Sometimes the answer to prayer arrives through an uncomfortable conversation.
Sometimes the shepherd sees the cliff before the sheep does.
The solution, therefore, is not:
“Ignore your pastor.”
Nor is it:
“Your pastor must approve everything.”
The biblical road is harder because it demands maturity.
Honor your leaders.
Receive correction.
Seek counsel.
Test teaching by Scripture.
Reject manipulation.
Reject rebellion.
Follow Jesus.
And never confuse the voice of a human shepherd with the voice of the Chief Shepherd.
There are times when a pastor may rightly say, “Scripture forbids what you are planning.”
In that case, the authority does not ultimately rest in the pastor’s preference.
It rests in God’s Word.
There are other times when a pastor may say, “Scripture does not explicitly forbid this, but based on what I know, I believe this is unwise.”
Take that seriously.
Very seriously.
You may discover later that the warning saved you years of pain.
But there is a difference between:
“I believe this would be unwise, and here is why.”
and
“God will punish you because you made a morally permissible personal decision without my permission.”
The first can be shepherding.
The second requires biblical evidence.
Whenever someone claims authority from God, Christians have every right—and responsibility—to ask:
Where does Scripture say that?
Not arrogantly.
Not mockingly.
Not rebelliously.
Humbly.
With an open Bible.
Because Scripture is not threatened by examination.
Neither is truth.
And neither should faithful Christian leadership be.
Maybe this article exposed something uncomfortable in you.
Perhaps you have been controlled.
Perhaps you have been rebellious.
Perhaps you have been afraid to make any decision without another person validating it.
Perhaps you have been calling stubbornness “discernment.”
Perhaps you are a leader and suddenly realize that somewhere along the way, shepherding quietly became controlling.
There is grace for that too.
This is the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely expose us.
He calls us home.
The controlling pastor can repent.
The rebellious Christian can repent.
The wounded believer can heal.
The frightened believer can learn to walk in wisdom.
The proud believer can become teachable.
The abused believer can rediscover healthy Christian community.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of people who got church leadership perfectly right.
It is the story of sinners rescued by a perfect Shepherd.
Jesus said:
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).
There He is.
The Shepherd who does not exploit His sheep.
The Shepherd who bleeds for them.
The Shepherd who does not manipulate people into protecting His position.
The Shepherd who surrendered Himself at Calvary.
The Shepherd who bore our scandal.
Our pride.
Our rebellion.
Our fear.
Our religious hypocrisy.
Our lust for control.
Our desperate need for human approval.
He carried it into death.
And then the stone moved.
The Shepherd lives.
So perhaps the question underneath this entire article was never merely:
“Do I need my pastor’s permission?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“Who truly owns my life?”
If the answer is Jesus, then you cannot use Christian freedom as permission for rebellion.
And nobody else can use Christian leadership as permission to possess you.
You are Christ’s.
That means you should become more humble, not less.
More teachable, not less.
More discerning, not less.
More accountable, not less.
More saturated in Scripture.
More willing to listen.
More willing to repent.
And more courageous when obedience to Christ costs you human approval.
Not because every disagreement with a pastor is abuse—it is not.
Both need Jesus.

One meaningful way believers can glorify God is through generous, voluntary support of sound Gospel work and by sharing truth with others; Scripture calls Christian giving willing rather than coerced (see 2 Corinthians 9:7).
But whatever you do after reading this, remember the truth beneath all of it:
A good pastor can counsel you.
A faithful pastor can warn you.
A biblical pastor can correct you.
A loving pastor can sometimes tell you something you desperately do not want to hear.
Honor that gift.
But the best pastors will eventually point beyond themselves and say:
“Follow Jesus.”
Because your pastor is a shepherd.
Jesus is the Shepherd.

And when every human voice has faded, every title has disappeared, every platform has fallen silent, and every earthly shepherd stands before God to give account, there will still be One with scars in His hands who purchased His people with His own blood.
Never give a human shepherd the throne that belongs to the Shepherd who died for you.
